messages.subject: Query Regarding Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Effects Model with Spatiotemporal Covariance Structure Using INLA
messages.subject_clean: Query Regarding Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Effects Model with Spatiotemporal Covariance Structure Using INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,
I am currently working on establishing a Bayesian generalized linear mixed effects model with a spatiotemporal covariance structure using the INLA package in R. My dataset has a non-temporal structure, meaning that the number and location of observation sites vary each year. To accommodate this variability, I have considered converting the data into panel format, generating dependent variable observations for all years from 2000 to 2019 and filling missing values with NA.
Here is my code:

stk.e <- inla.stack(
  tag = "est",
  data = list(y = C_Y_T$Y),
  A = list(1, A_SAM),
  effects = list(data.frame(b0 = 1, X1=C_Y_T$ID), s = w.index)
)

rprior1 <- list(theta = list(prior = 'loggamma', param = c(1, 0.02)), theta1 = list(prior = 'normal', param = c(0, 1/(2^2))))
formula <- y ~ X1 + f(w, model = spde.sp, group = w.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1", hyper = rprior1))

res <- inla(formula,
            family = "gaussian",
            data = inla.stack.data(stk.e),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.e), compute = TRUE),
            control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, config = TRUE),
            control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),
            verbose = TRUE
)

When I run the code, I received the warnings and errors:

My question is whether the INLA model can handle such a dataset with missing values (NA) appropriately, or if it will automatically remove these missing values during the model fitting process. I would like to understand whether INLA can deal with datasets where the observation sites are not consistent across time points and how this might affect the model's performance and results.

Any help will be greatly appreciated.

Best wishes,

messages.subject: Long preparation time for custom Cmatrix for Leroux prior
messages.subject_clean: Long preparation time for custom Cmatrix for Leroux prior
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am fitting spatial models with a Cmatrix to apply Leroux prior against a spatial dataset with 50K rows and 6 covariates.

```
library(INLA)
library(spdep)
library(sf)
options(num.threads = "8:3", smtp = "taucs", sf_use_s2 = FALSE)
## INLA settings ####
control_inla_custom <-
  list(
    restart = 5L,
    npoints = 21,
    cutoff = 5e-06,
    stupid.search.max.iter = 3000L,
    stupid.search.factor = 1.01,
    #improved.simplified.laplace = TRUE,
    strategy = "simplified.laplace"
  )
control_compute_custom <-
  list(
    # openmp.strategy = "huge",
    return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,
    dic = TRUE,
    cpo = TRUE,
    waic = TRUE,
    residuals = TRUE
  )

sdunif <- "expression:
logdens=-log_precision/2;
return(logdens)"

## Create the matrix for Leroux prior
make_leroux_matrix <-
  function(graph, input_r) {
    g <- inla.read.graph(graph)
    Rs <- matrix(0, g$n, g$n)
    for (i in 1:g$n) {
      Rs[i, i] <- g$nnbs[[i]]
      Rs[i, g$nbs[[i]]] <- -1
    }
    R_Leroux <- diag(dim(input_r)[1]) - Rs
    return(R_Leroux)
  }

lerouxC <- make_leroux_matrix(graph_path_18, sf_tracts)

compact_inla <-
  function(data, cmat = lerouxC, prior = sdunif) {
  formula_base <- outcome ~ 1 +
  f(ID.area, model = "generic1", Cmatrix = cmat, constr = TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = prior))) +
  f(state, model = "iid", hyper = list(prec = list(prior = prior)), constr = TRUE) + p_pct_black + p_pct_65p + depriv + p_mobility + d_log_pop_sqkm

  form_sel <- update(formula_base, .~.+close_4_0005_r_100k_ter)

  fit_inla <-
    INLA::inla(
      formula = form_sel,
      data = data,
      verbose = TRUE,
      control.compute = control_compute_custom,
      control.inla = control_inla_custom
    )
  return(fit_inla)
  }
```
It was fitted after 1.5 hours, of which around 99% of fitting time spent in preparation stage.

```
Store results in directory[/tmp/RtmpnYJAQg/file240abc4ccd9487/results.files]

Wall-clock time used on [/tmp/RtmpnYJAQg/file240abc4ccd9487/Model.ini]
        Preparations             : 4562.138 seconds
        Approx inference (stage1):  58.045 seconds
        Approx inference (stage2):   0.004 seconds
        Approx inference (total) :  58.049 seconds
        Output                   :   1.874 seconds
        ------------------------------------------
        Total                    : 4622.061 seconds

Stage1: Number of fn-calls= 1141 with 0.0509 sec/fn-call
Stage2: Number of fn-calls= 0 with 58.0489 sec/fn-call
Stage1: Accumulated CPU-time is equivalent to 1.26 threads running at 100%
        Efficiency using 24 threads = 5.24%
Stage2: Accumulated CPU-time is equivalent to 1.00 threads running at 100%
        Efficiency using 24 threads = 4.17%
Total:  Accumulated CPU-time is equivalent to 1.26 threads running at 100%
        Efficiency using 24 threads = 5.24%
```

Is it a normal behavior? I am wondering if there is a way to reduce the preparation time.

Thank you very much.
Best,
Insang Song

messages.subject: Help with computational issues R-INLA
messages.subject_clean: Help with computational issues R-INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone. I'm working on a master thesis project, and my goal is to compute predictions for NO₂ concentrations in the Po Valley. I have a dataset with daily records measured by 168 stations located in the designated area (dati_completi_df).

My data contain the following information:
mean_NO₂: the response variable
Altitude, Longitude, Latitude
mean_NO₂_c: NO₂ concentrations measured by Copernicus.
Date: a variable indicating the day of measurement
AirQualityStationEoICode: an identifier for each station
I also built a prediction grid (grigliato_previsione) with the same information, except for the AirQualityStationEoICode, which I would like to use to build prediction maps.

Here is my code, which is based on Blangiardo, Micheletti (2015) example for PM10 predictions in Piemonte:

train_sf <- dati_completi_df |>
  dplyr::filter(Date < "2023-12-01")  # train set from 2023-01-01 to 2023-11-30

test_sf <- dati_completi_df |>
  dplyr::filter(Date >= "2023-12-01") # test set from 2023-12-01 to 2023-12-31

n_station <- length(unique(train_sf$AirQualityStationEoICode))
n_data <- nrow(train_sf)
n_days <- n_data/n_station

train_sf$time <- rep(1:n_days, times = n_station)

coordinates.allyear <- as.matrix(train_sf[, c("Longitude", "Latitude")] |>
                                   st_drop_geometry())

limiti <- st_coordinates(contorno)[, c("X", "Y")]  #contorno is an sf object containing the area of interest

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = coordinates.allyear,
                     loc.domain = limiti,
                     offset = c(0.3, 0.5),
                     max.edge = c(0.5, 1))

mesh$n #699

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2)

A_est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh,
                          loc = coordinates.allyear,
                          group = train_sf$time,
                          n.group = n_days)

dim(A_est)   # 56112  233466

s_index <- inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field",
                                n.spde = spde$n.spde,
                                n.group = n_days)

stack_est <- inla.stack(data = list(mean_NO2 = train_sf$mean_NO2),
                        A = list(A_est, 1),
                        effects = list(c(s_index,list(Intercept = 1)),
                                     list(data.frame(Altitude = train_sf$Altitude,
                                            mean_NO2_c = train_sf$mean_NO2_c))),
                        tag = "est")

grigliato_previsione$time <- rep(1:length(unique(grigliato_previsione$Date)),
                                 times = length(unique(grigliato_previsione$ID)))

gg <- grigliato_previsione |>
  dplyr::filter(time %in% 335:365)

gg <- gg[1, ] # prediction only on one point and one time stamp

A_pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh,
                           loc = cbind(gg$Longitude, gg$Latitude),
                           group = gg$time,
                           n.group = n_days + length(unique(gg$time)))

dim(A_pred) # 1  234165

s_index_pred <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field",
                                     n.spde = spde$n.spde,
                                     n.group = n_days + length(unique(gg$time)))

stack_pred <- inla.stack(data = list(mean_NO2 = NA),
                         A = list(A_pred, 1),
                         effects = list(c(s_index_pred, list(Intercept = 1)),
                                      list(data.frame(Altitude = gg$Altitude,
                                                      mean_NO2_c = gg$mean_NO2_c))),
                         tag = "pred")

stack <- inla.stack(stack_est, stack_pred)

formula <- mean_NO2 ~ -1 + Intercept + f(spatial.field, model = spde,
                          group = spatial.field.group, control.group = list(model = "rw1")) +
  Altitude + mean_NO2_c

output <- inla(formula,
               data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde = spde),
               family ="gaussian", quantiles = NULL,
               control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE),
               control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = F),
               control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", int.strategy = "ccd"),
               num.threads = 2)

output

My model takes AGES just to predict one point at one time stamp and I'm a little bit discouraged. Do you have any suggestion? Am I doing something wrong? I'm not so familiar with the R-INLA package.

Thank you so much in advance,
Alessia

messages.subject_clean: Making predictions for spatial model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm fitting a BYM2 model using the Poisson distribution. In the data, I have "SES" as a factor covariate and "ID" as the spatial index column. I'm interested in making predictions at various SES levels (1 to 5). I understand that I need to refit the BYM2 model, including additional rows with y = NA for making predictions.

The additional rows look like:
|y  |SES |     var2|     var3|   var4|ID |
|:--|:---|--------:|--------:|------:|:--|
|NA |1   | 46.01933| 12.98228| 29.407|NA |
|NA |2   | 46.01933| 12.98228| 29.407|NA |
|NA |3   | 46.01933| 12.98228| 29.407|NA |
|NA |4   | 46.01933| 12.98228| 29.407|NA |
|NA |5   | 46.01933| 12.98228| 29.407|NA |
Here, var2, var3, var4 are other covariates and I simply set them as the mean value.

Since I'm not concerned about making predictions at specific geographies, I want to know what the predictions actually represent when I set ID = NA?

Further, I would like to estimate the "absolute difference" of the predicted values between SES = 2 to 5 vs SES = 1. I also need the credible intervals of the difference. How can I (or if it even makes sense to) make use of the marginals.fitted.values associated with the predicted entries to derive the "absolute difference" and credible intervals?

Hana

compact_inla <-
  function(data, cmat = lerouxC, prior = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))) {
  formula_base <- outcome~ 1 +
  f(ID.area, model = "generic1", Cmatrix = cmat, constr = TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(5, 0.01)))) +

  f(state, model = "iid", hyper = list(prec = list(prior = prior)), constr = TRUE) + p_pct_black + p_pct_65p + depriv + p_mobility + d_log_pop_sqkm

    INLA::inla(

      data = data,
      verbose = TRUE,
      control.compute = control_compute_custom,
      control.inla = control_inla_custom
    )
  return(fit_inla)
  }

messages.subject: What is mlik really equal to?
messages.subject_clean: What is mlik really equal to?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

What is mlik really equal to ?
Reasons for this silly question are :
mlik stands for marginal likelihood. But its value is given on log scale. Hence, it is actually the log marginal likelihood ;
In the R-dlm package, the function dlmLL <https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dlm/versions/1.1-6.1/topics/dlmLL> is described as "Function that computes the log likelihood of a state space model." but the value is defined as "The function returns the negative of the loglikelihood" ;
With R-dlm, I'm estimating nested models by iteratively adding parameters e.g. for taking into account appropriately outliers (i.e. nor false or doubtful data, but really exceptional) ; mechanically, the log-likelihoods of these models increase;
With R-INLA, I'm doing the same thing, but the mlik (on a log scale) are decreasing.
I'm taking outliers into account as describe here :
https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/c3-MyeIijFE/m/k8fp62FfAgAJ
Thanks in advance
Regards
DS

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What is mlik really equal to?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] What is mlik really equal to?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
When you say in point 3 that “mechanically, the log-likelihoods of these models increase “ I think you’re mistaken. The marginal “likelihood” in the Bayesian setting is the joint pdf/pmf for observations and unknowns integrated over the unknowns,
p(y) = int  p(y,theta) d\theta = int p(y|theta) p(theta) d\theta
When you you expand the model with more parameters, you’re increasing the flexibility of the model to generate different data, and unless the priors are changed in certain ways as well, you’re likely to end up with a smaller value for p(y), as your particular observation is less probable in the expanded model.

In frequentist settings, one instead commonly considers the maximum likelihood value instead, which can have a very different behaviour to the integrated likelihood.

(Also, the marginal likelihood isn’t actually a likelihood; the likelihood is the observation density seen as a function of the parameters, which isn’t the same thing as the joint, conditional, or marginal densities. I’m not sure who started using this misleading terminology in the Bayesian literature, but unfortunately it seems we have to live with it…)

Finn

messages.subject: Assistance Needed with Seasonality Modelling in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Assistance Needed with Seasonality Modelling in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA Community,

I am reaching out to seek assistance in properly framing a seasonality model using INLA. I am relatively new to this framework and am eager to learn. While I have found various online resources, I am struggling with understanding the implementation of a seasonality model.

I have referred to INLA::inla.doc("seasonal") and reviewed discussions such as this thread  https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/31_a_RcBC-U, but I still find some aspects unclear.

Model Description:

I am working with a dataset consisting of monthly records indicating the presence or absence of an event, along with relevant variables. I have gaps in the time series, meaning that my data cover just a few random months every year.  The data includes repeated measures at each location, which are not spatially correlated. Each location is uniquely identified by a code. Here is a sample of my data:

  time_step Month  Year Region Country smllcnt Place     Code           Y tmean_lag0

      <int> <int> <int> <chr>  <chr>     <int> <chr>     <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>

       201     3  2023 Africa Réunion       1 Réunion   REU            0       297.

       67     1  2012 Europe Germany       0 Ahrweiler DEU.11.1_1     0       276.

       69     3  2012 Europe Germany       0 Ahrweiler DEU.11.1_1     0       281.

      94     4  2014 Europe Germany       0 Ahrweiler DEU.11.1_1     0       284.

       96     6  2014 Europe Germany       0 Ahrweiler DEU.11.1_1     0       288.

      116     2  2016 Europe Germany       0 Ahrweiler DEU.11.1_1     0       276.

I aim to construct a binomial model that accounts for seasonality and includes random effects for location. To address seasonality despite gaps, I created a "time_step" index spanning all months and years from the earliest to the latest date. This index starts at 1 (2006-07-01) and ends at 210 (2023-12-01).

Model Structure:

Here is my attempt at coding this in R using INLA:

baseformula = Y ~ 1 + f(Code, model = "iid") + f(time_step, model = "seasonal", season.length = 12)

res = inla(baseformula, family = 'binomial', data = data,

           Ntrials = 1,

           control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),

           control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, return.marginals.predictor = TRUE))

 Questions:

·         Is this the proper way to include seasonality in my model?

·         How can I validate the seasonal assumption?

·         Will this approach allow me to make predictions for missing and future time steps?

I would greatly appreciate any guidance or suggestions. Thank you!

Best regards,

messages.body_plain:
for a NA observation, you need to set the argument 'link' to 'i' to say that
this NA is related to the i'th likelihood. Otherwise, you can map it yourself,
using the function inla.tmarginal  and inla.zmarginal

n = 100
z = runif(n)
eta = 1 + 0.1*z
N = 10

## logit
p = exp(eta)/(1+exp(eta))
y = rbinom(n,  size = N, prob = p)
y[(n-10):n] = NA
r = inla(y ~ 1 + z,  data = data.frame(y, z), family = "binomial", Ntrials =
rep(N, n),
    control.family = list(control.link = list(model = "logit")),
    control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))

rr = inla(y ~ 1 + z,  data = data.frame(y, z), family = "binomial", Ntrials =
rep(N, n),
    control.family = list(control.link = list(model = "logit")),
    control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE, link=1))

rrr = inla(y ~ 1 + z,  data = data.frame(y, z), family = "binomial", Ntrials =
rep(N, n),
    control.family = list(control.link = list(model = "logit")),
    control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE, link=NA))

tail(cbind(r$summary.fitted.values$mean, rr$summary.fitted.values$mean,
rrr$summary.fitted.values$mean))

messages.subject: Advice for limiting pseudo-replication when applying INLA framework to ecological data
messages.subject_clean: Advice for limiting pseudo-replication when applying INLA framework to ecological data
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I'm working on a project that involves assessing the habitat preferences of an animal species using a dataset of presences and absences. In other words, the fundamental model has a binary response (either the animal was seen as part of that observation, or it was not) and predictors that measure qualities about the animals' environments and what not. I also plan on including a spatial random effect following the SPDE notation.

The problem is that I'm almost certain there are significant issues with pseudoreplication in the dataset. For example, there may be observations of the same individual animal only a few minutes apart at the same location: an obvious pseudoreplication problem. One option is to remove data from the dataset, but I'd like to find an intelligent way to handle this and maybe retain a bit more statistical power / effective sample size. I think some sort of spatiotemporal model may be able to handle this, although there could also be observations at similar times and very different places (i.e., of different individual animals), so I'd need to think a bit harder about exactly what form is desirable.

An example of an approach that can work under certain assumptions is described here <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025> but this does not use INLA. In short, they performed a sort of weighted regression where the likelihood weights associated with each data point were generated according to autocorrelation within the data, such that two locations at a very similar location and time had weights closer to 0.5. They achieved this using a sort of two-step modelling process; ideally I'd like something that can be done all in one swoop with INLA but I'm not sure if it's possible.

If it helps, I can provide a short code example of the existing model I'm working with, where pseudoreplication is a problem. But before that, I figured I'd ask about this from a more philosophical standpoint, in case there are some applications of INLA that I'm not aware of that could work here.

Thank you in advance for any help you might be able to provide,
Peter

reading what you write, then in space-time, with a time-model for movement, then
you should be able to do similarly?

so two observation with similar time will be dependent, while two with long time
inbetween will not be (dependence in the log\lambda)

a simple choice could be a simple AR1 in time added to the SPDE + covariates ?

Maybe other have some ideas...

Best
H

The "composite likelihood" in their equation (5) is just a version of
the regular inhomogeneous Poisson point process (IHPPP) likelihood
that puts a weight on each observed point.
This is in principle easy to implement by just slightly adjusting the
code for regular IHPPP models, as implemented in the
inlabru::bru_obs() function.
Instead of counting each point as "1" point, one would just need to
supply the weight values to use instead.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Likely the easiest way to do this at the moment would be to fork the
inlabru repository and make a branch where a special point_weight
argument is added to the bru_obs() method, to be used in the "cp"
model likelihood implemented there.
I'm in the process of modularising bru_obs() to make implementing such
special likelihoods a bit easier, but at the moment, adjusting
bru_obs() is the easiest approach, I think.

I'm less convinced of the "add an AR(1) model" approach, as I think
that would require more fundamental changes to the observation model.

Finn

I guess you mean f(x, model ="iid", constr=TRUE)

constr=T will say that the sum (or mean), of the iid effects are set to zero,
hence the iid effects are centered. this would ensure, f.ex. that a model

	1 + f(x, model="iid", constr=TRUE)

has no confounding between the intercept and iid terms

messages.subject: Seeking assistance with spatial modelling
messages.subject_clean: Seeking assistance with spatial modelling
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA experts,

I'm currently attempting to fit the following model using inlabru with simulated data, the model after log-transform is:

log(U) ~ offset + X + 3log(H) + log(H+beta)

where U is the response variable, X is a covariate, H and beta are 1D spatial random effects to be determined.

However, if I just use the following code, it gives an error because log(H) is only defined for positive H. How do I specify so that H is always positive?

x <- seq(0, 5000, by = 20)
mesh1D <- fm_mesh_1d(x, boundary = "free")

H_spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh1D,
  prior.range = c(20, 0.01),
  prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01)
)

beta_spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh1D,
  prior.range = c(20, 0.01),
  prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01)
)

I0.bru <- bru(components = ~ H(x, model = H_spde) + beta(x, model = beta_spde),
  bru_obs(us ~ offset(-11.22) + X + 3*log(H) + log(H+beta),
    data = data0,
    family = "gaussian",
    control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 4, fixed = TRUE)))),
)

Many thanks,
Minghao

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Seeking assistance with spatial modelling
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Seeking assistance with spatial modelling
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Since inla model consist of latent Gaussian variables, they are fundamentally not limited to positive values. The most common technique for things like log(H) is to let log(H) itself be the Gaussian field, or to use some other transformation to take a Gaussian field to H (e.g. if you want more specific control over the marginal distribution of H than a log-Normal. In your case, you’d also need to handle beta in this way. You can define components logH and logbeta and use logH + log(exp(logH)+exp(logbeta)) in the predictor expression.

I should also define the offset as a “constant component” so that inlabru can handle it properly;
  myoffset(-11.22, model=“const”) + logH(…) + logbeta(…)
in the component definitions, and
  myoffset  + 3*logH + log(exp(logH)+exp(logbeta))
in the formula, or simply subtract 11.22 in the formula without defining it as a component or offset; the formula is just a regular R expression.

Finn

messages.subject: Fitting spatial model with two SPDEs
messages.subject_clean: Fitting spatial model with two SPDEs
messages.body_plain:
Hello!
I am trying to fit a spatial model using two spatial fields. In essence, I am assuming that there are two underlying spatial "states", and each year in my dataset is a linear combination of these two states. A crude representation of what I want to do would be:

formula <- obs ~ -1 +
year : f(spatial.field1, model = spde1_mod4) +
year : f(spatial.field2, model = spde2_mod4)

Though I am aware that I cannot specify the interaction like this. I'm not sure if I can use the 'group' argument, since I don't want the actual spatial field to vary between years, just an overall coefficient that will be applied to the entire spatial field. Is there a way to implement this in R-INLA?

Thank you!!

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Fitting spatial model with two SPDEs
messages.body_plain:
As far as I understand you, then you have replicated measurement of the two
fields over years, then you could write them as

	a * field.1 + (1-a) * field.2
or
	s * ( \sqrt{a} * field.1 + \sqrt{(1-a)} * field.2)   (*)

as you see, then the variances of field.1 and 2 are confounded with 'a', hence
this can be achived with

	field.1 + field.2

and the 'a' follows from the variances. the  (*) representation would require
that the variances of field.1 and 2 are fixed, like = 1, then s^2 is the overall
variances, and 'a' in (*) is the variance particion. (see
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16057  for a recent treatment of variance particion)
